summary: The Network Information Center explains why it favors standard host names and what a good scheme should do. It suggests names made of a site part and a host part separated by a delimiter, easy to remember, and at least eight characters long. It was replaced by RFC 273.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 237 presents the NIC's view of a standard host-name format. It recommends names with site and host parts and asks the NWG to set a shared syntax.

questions: host naming scheme site and host
what host naming scheme did the nic recommend
subtitle: The NIC's 1971 recommendations for a standard form of network host name.

tldr.problem: Different host names could be used in NIC documents and Telnet, making it harder for users to identify the same host consistently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 237 recommends names with SITE and HOST parts, preferably separated by a delimiter, and says names should be mnemonic and allow at least eight characters.
tldr.outcome: The note recommends that the NIC maintain a naming standard and assign names to hosts and other network participants. It was later obsoleted by RFC 273.

today: RFC 237 is historic and was obsoleted by RFC 273. It records the NIC's recommendations for standard host names in the ARPANET.

sections.title: Why Standard Host Names Were Needed
sections.content: The Network Information Center (NIC) favored standard host names so the names used in NIC documents would agree with names used in Telnet. RFC 237 says users could become confused when the names differed.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC wanted a host's name in its documents to match the name users typed in Telnet. Different names for the same host could cause confusion.

sections.title: The Suggested Name Structure
sections.content: The NIC recommends two parts, SITE and HOST, preferably separated by a delimiter such as a dash. It prefers mnemonic names that refer to the organization rather than the computer model, because the computer may change while the organization remains. It recommends allowing at least eight characters including the delimiter.
sections.plainLanguage: A name should show both the site and the host. The NIC preferred meaningful names that were not tied to a computer model.

sections.title: Maintaining the Names
sections.content: For an eight-character name, the document recommends a site name of at most six characters and host names unique within a site in their first six characters. It proposes that, after the NWG sets syntax and names, the NIC maintain the standard and assign names to new hosts and other network participants.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal asks the NWG to set the naming rules and the NIC to maintain them. Host names at one site should remain distinguishable even when shortened to six characters.
